name: room
text: Room opened — goal: improve: Self-improvement: review prompts/engines/routing/own-code; auto-apply safe changes; pitch

name: Sprocket
text:
Do: Replace the current prompt-review system with a shared log that records every change to prompts, engines, or routing rules.

This gives us a single source of truth for all improvements, making it easy to track what changed, why, and who approved it. The trade-off is that we lose the ability to revert changes quickly without the log, but the log itself becomes the revert mechanism—every change is documented and reversible by design.

name: Gauge
text: A shared log risks becoming a graveyard of stale noise—changes pile up, reasons blur, and no one reads it. Instead, auto-apply safe changes with a lightweight review step: only deviations or high-risk edits trigger human scrutiny. Settle it by testing both: measure how often the log is referenced vs. how often auto-applied changes are rolled back.

name: Sprocket
text:
Do: Auto-apply safe changes to prompts, engines, and routing rules—only flag high-risk edits for human review. This keeps the system moving fast while preventing obvious mistakes from piling up. The trade-off is that we risk missing subtle misalignments, but the cost of slowing down every change outweighs the risk of a rare bad edit.

name: Gauge
text: Auto-applying safe changes still risks a cascade of silent misalignments—what’s “safe” today may break tomorrow as context shifts. Instead, set a hard rule: auto-apply only if the change passes a regression test suite, and require a human sign-off for any deviation from past behavior. Settle it by running both methods in parallel for two weeks and comparing error rates in production.
